name: Khoisan peoples (San and Khoekhoe)
summary: The San hunter-gatherers and Khoekhoe herders of southern Africa, whose ancestors have lived there for tens of thousands of years. Their rock art is among the oldest art traditions on Earth. They were not one state but many small groups.

knownFor.label: San rock art
knownFor.note: Thousands of paintings and engravings of animals, people and rituals, some many thousands of years old.

knownFor.label: Click languages
knownFor.note: Languages that use click sounds as consonants.

knownFor.label: Persistence hunting
knownFor.note: Tracking and running down animals in the heat of the day.

location.value: Southern Africa: the Kalahari, the Cape, Namibia, Botswana and once much of eastern Africa too.

terrain.value: Deserts, dry savannah, coastal plains and mountains (Drakensberg).

climate.value: Mostly dry; winter rain at the Cape, summer rain further north.

resources.value: Wild plants, game, water holes; the Khoekhoe later kept sheep and cattle.

urbanisation.value: No towns; camps of a few dozen people.

disease.value: The 1713 smallpox epidemic at the Cape killed a large share of the Khoekhoe.

migration.value: Bantu-speaking farmers moved into the region from about 300 CE; Dutch settlers arrived in 1652.

economicBase.value: San: hunting and gathering. Khoekhoe: herding sheep and cattle (from about 2,000 years ago).

tradeRoutes.value: Exchanged goods with Bantu-speaking farmers and later with European ships at the Cape.

wealth.value: Little private wealth among the San, who valued sharing; Khoekhoe wealth was counted in cattle.

inequality.value: San bands were very equal; Khoekhoe chiefs had more wealth.

governmentType.value: No state: San bands led by consensus; Khoekhoe clans and chiefdoms.

keyRulers.value: No recorded rulers in early times; Khoekhoe leaders such as Autshumao dealt with the Dutch (1650s).

succession.value: Leadership by respected elders; Khoekhoe chiefs could be hereditary.

institutions.value: Sharing customs, trance dances and kinship rules.

stability.value: Groups split and moved as needed.

eliteConflict.value: Disputes were often settled by groups moving apart.

majorWars.value: Khoikhoi–Dutch Wars (1659–1677); violence on the Cape frontier in the 18th–19th centuries.

territoryChange.value: Lost most of their land to farmers and colonists.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded and intermarried with Bantu-speaking neighbours, such as the Xhosa.

inventions.value: Arrow poisons from beetle larvae; ostrich-eggshell water containers; plant medicines.

scienceEducation.value: Deep knowledge of plants, animals and tracking passed on orally.

openness.value: Mobile and open, sharing knowledge with neighbours.

religion.value: Spiritual beliefs centred on healers, trance dances and animals such as the eland.

languageWriting.value: Khoe and San languages with clicks; some click sounds were borrowed into Xhosa and Zulu.

artsArchitecture.value: Rock paintings and engravings across southern Africa; beadwork from ostrich eggshell.

socialStructure.value: Small, very equal bands among the San.

sharedIdentity.value: Identity built around kin groups, language and land.

neighbours.value: Bantu-speaking peoples, later Dutch and British colonists.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity spread through missions from the 18th century.

colonisation.value: Colonised by the Dutch and British; many Khoekhoe were absorbed into the Cape Coloured community.

riseSignals.value: Successful survival in harsh environments over very long periods.

peakPeriod.value: No single peak; the San once lived across most of southern and eastern Africa.

declineSignals.value: Loss of land, disease and violence after 1652.

outcome.value: San and Khoekhoe communities still exist in Namibia, Botswana and South Africa.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Khoisan; Wikipedia: San people; Barnard, Hunters and Herders of Southern Africa (1992).

overallCertainty.value: Mostly known from archaeology, genetics and colonial records; dates are approximate.
